Completeness for Probabilistic Boolean Tapes
Filippo Bonchi, Cipriano Junior Cioffo

Abstract
Probabilistic Boolean circuits have recently been proposed as a string-diagrammatic foundation for finite probabilistic programming. In this paper, we present a complete set of axioms for their semantics in terms of Markov kernels. Our approach is based on two intermediate results: completeness for partial Boolean circuits and completeness for probabilistic Boolean tapes, a diagrammatic language for rig categories.

Introduction

Diagrammatic languages play a central role in computer science, with classical examples including Petri nets, graph rewriting systems
[
22
,
28
]
, and data- and control-flow diagrams
[
5
]
, among others.
More recently, the increasing importance of spatial structure in computation led Milner to move beyond the traditional term-based syntax of process calculi and introduce bigraphs
[
52
]
. Similar trends arise in quantum computing
[
62
,
24
,
1
,
19
,
3
,
38
]
and probabilistic programming
[
48
,
25
,
61
,
67
,
50
]
, where–unlike in classical computation–information cannot be freely copied or discarded. More broadly, the shift towards viewing data as a physical resource rather than a purely logical entity (see, e.g.,
[
57
,
36
]
) has driven the widespread adoption
[
4
,
13
,
15
,
29
,
30
,
37
,
54
,
60
,
12
,
17
,
43
,
59
,
11
,
27
,
26
,
44
,
53
,
33
,
32
,
35
,
67
,
58
,
34
,
31
]
of
string diagrams

[
46
,
64
]
as a graphical syntax.

Formally, string diagrams are morphisms in the symmetric monoidal category freely generated by a monoidal signature
\Sigma
, which we denote by
\mathbf{Diag}_{\Sigma}
. The signature contains a basic set of generating symbols and complex diagrams are built via horizontal (
;
) and vertical (
\otimes
) composition. Such diagrams are typically interpreted in a monoidal category
\mathbf{C}
via a map
\langle\!\langle{\cdot}\rangle\!\rangle\colon\mathbf{Diag}_{\Sigma}\to\mathbf{C}
assigning semantics to each diagram. When
\langle\!\langle{\cdot}\rangle\!\rangle
is a monoidal functor–i.e., it preserves both
;
and
\otimes
–the semantics is compositional, and the induced notion of semantic equality forms a congruence. Axiomatizing this congruence is a central challenge, as it enables equational reasoning directly at the level of diagrams.

In this paper, we provide a complete axiomatisation of
probabilistic Boolean circuits

[
59
]
. These circuits are string diagrams generated by the following monoidal signature, where
p
belongs to
(0,1)
.

(PrB)

The first three generators are the standard Boolean gates:
takes two inputs and returns their conjunction;
maps an input to its negation; and
1
produces the constant
1
. The generator
duplicates its input, while
discards it. The gate
can be seen as a dual of
: it takes two inputs and returns their common value if they agree, and otherwise fails. Finally,
p
is a probabilistic generator that outputs
1
with probability
p
and
0
with probability
1-p
.
A circuit
c
with
n
inputs and
m
outputs denotes a function
\langle\!\langle{c}\rangle\!\rangle\colon 2^{n}\to\mathcal{D}_{\leq}(2^{m})
, where
2=\{0,1\}
and
\mathcal{D}_{\leq}(X)
is the set of subdistributions over
X
. Categorically, the semantics
\langle\!\langle{\cdot}\rangle\!\rangle
is a functor from
\mathbf{Diag}_{PrB}
, the category of probabilistic circuits, to
\mathcal{KL}(\mathcal{D}_{\leq})
, the Kleisli category of the subdistribution monad (see e.g.
[
40
]
).

The brace below (
PrB
) highlights an important fragment: diagrams in
\mathbf{Diag}_{B}
correspond to standard Boolean circuits, hence denote Boolean functions. As such, they can be freely copied and discarded, meaning respectively that the following equalities hold:

While we refer the reader to
[
59
]
for a discussion of the practical relevance of this formalism, we emphasise here the advantages of diagrammatic syntax over traditional term-based representations. Standard Boolean identities fail in the probabilistic setting–for instance,
x\wedge x=x
does not hold when
x\in\mathcal{D}(2)
. However, these laws hold in diagrammatic form, where copying and discarding are made explicit; see, e.g., (
1
) in
Figure

1
. The latter collects the axioms of Boolean algebra which, as shown in
[
59
]
, yields a complete axiomatisation of the Boolean fragment
\mathbf{Diag}_{B}
.

Our first contribution is a complete axiomatisation of partial Boolean circuits, i.e., circuits in
\mathbf{Diag}_{PB}
. The axioms extend those of Boolean algebra in
Figure

1
with additional laws governing
, presented in
Figure

3
. Completeness –in Theorem
9
– is crucial for the second contribution.

For the full language, rather than axiomatise
\mathbf{Diag}_{PrB}
directly, we consider a more expressive formalism–
probabilistic Boolean tapes
– which as illustrated in
[
8
, Ex. 30]
can faithfully express probabilistic Boolean circuits. Probabilistic Boolean tapes arise from a general construction applied to partial Boolean circuits. Concretely, by freely adding
convex biproducts
to
\mathbf{Diag}_{PB}
, we obtain a category
\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{PB})
representing the syntax, together with a semantic map
\left\llbracket\cdot\right\rrbracket\colon\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{PB})\to\mathcal{KL}(\mathcal{D}_{\leq})

extending
\langle\!\langle{\cdot}\rangle\!\rangle\colon\mathbf{Diag}_{PB}\to\mathcal{KL}(\mathcal{D}_{\leq})
.
Crucially,
\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{PB})
is, like
\mathcal{KL}(\mathcal{D}_{\leq})
, a
rig category

[
49
,
45
]
, featuring two monoidal structures:
\otimes
and
\oplus
. Moreover,
\left\llbracket\cdot\right\rrbracket
is a morphism of rig categories, i.e. it preserves
;
,
\otimes
and
\oplus
. As a consequence, the semantics remains compositional.
Finally, probabilistic Boolean tapes admit an intuitive graphical syntax, closely related to string diagrams. The raison d’être of tape diagrams
[
10
]
is precisely to represent the three forms of composition–
\otimes
,
\oplus
, and
;
–uniformly within two dimensions, rather than requiring an additional dimension as e.g. in
[
21
]
.

The move from circuits to tapes allows us to reason not only about the monoidal product
\otimes
in
\mathcal{KL}(\mathcal{D}_{\leq})
, but also about the operation
\oplus
, which plays a fundamental role in many probabilistic frameworks
[
67
,
18
,
50
]
. As discussed in Example
13
, the presence of
\oplus
provides a natural way of modelling probabilistic control and, perhaps more importantly, leads to a structurally transparent axiomatisation. In addition to the equalities induced by the tape construction in
Figure

4
, our axiomatisation comprises the three additional laws shown in Figure
5
. The third of these is an implication expressing
cancellativity
. Although not purely equational, cancellativity is a standard reasoning principle that arises naturally in a wide variety of algebraic structures.

Relying on completeness for partial Boolean circuits and on a result from
[
6
]
–stated here as
Corollary

18
–characterising tape diagrams as stochastic matrices of string diagrams, we prove completeness for probabilistic Boolean tapes in
Corollary

29
. Consequently, as stated in
Corollary

30
, semantic equality of probabilistic Boolean circuits reduces to equality of their encodings as tapes.

Related Work.
Figures 4 and 5 of
[
59
]
provide an axiomatisation of probabilistic Boolean circuits. Crucially, the induced equivalence is strictly coarser than semantic equality, i.e., the one induced by
\langle\!\langle{-}\rangle\!\rangle
. In fact, two diagrams
c
and
d
are equivalent in
[
59
]
if and only if
\langle\!\langle{c}\rangle\!\rangle\propto\langle\!\langle{d}\rangle\!\rangle
, where
\propto
is the relation on
\mathcal{KL}(\mathcal{D}_{\leq})
defined by
f\propto g
whenever there exists
\lambda>0
such that

f(x)(y)=\lambda\cdot g(x)(y)
for all
x\in X
and
y\in Y
.
Hence, several axioms in
[
59
]
–in particular F2 and F7–are unsound with respect to
\langle\!\langle{\cdot}\rangle\!\rangle
. Interestingly, as shown in
Lemma

4
, axiom F8 of
[
59
]
is derivable from our system.

To the best of our knowledge, partial Boolean circuits have not previously been axiomatised. In contrast,
[
59
]
gives a complete axiomatisation for the
causal
fragment, i.e., circuits generated by all gates in (
PrB
) except
. In
[
6
]
, the characterisation of tapes as stochastic matrices is used to derive an alternative axiomatisation for the same fragment.
Despite exploiting the same result, the two axiomatisations differ substantially. Indeed, among all the axioms in Figures
3
and
5
, (T3) is the only one that is even expressible with the tapes in
[
6
]
.

Synopsis.
Our presentation of probabilistic Boolean circuits is staged: we begin in
Section

2
with
\mathbf{Diag}_{B}
, then
\mathbf{Diag}_{PB}
in

Section

3
and finally
\mathbf{Diag}_{PrB}
in
Section

4
. Hence, the axiomatisation for partial Boolean circuits and its proof of completeness are illustrated in
Section

3
.
Section

5
recalls from
[
8
]
probabilistic Boolean tapes as well as the encoding of circuits into tapes;
Section

6
illustrates several general results from
[
6
]
about the tape construction. These are used in
Section

7
to provide a complete axiomatisation of probabilistic Boolean tapes and prove its completeness. All missing proofs are in the appendices. Appendix
A
contains additional material: in particular the axioms in Table
3
already appear in the form of tapes in
Figure

4
in the main text.

2
Boolean Circuits

We commence our exposition by recalling how Boolean circuits can be regarded as string diagrams.

A
monoidal signature
is a tuple
(\mathcal{S},\Sigma,\mathit{ar},\mathit{coar})
where
\mathcal{S}
is a set of basic sorts, hereafter denoted by
A,B,\dots
,
\Sigma
is a set of generators, denoted by
s,t,\dots
, and
\mathit{ar},\mathit{coar}\colon\Sigma\to\mathcal{S}^{*}
assign to each symbol its arity and coarity, i.e., words over
\mathcal{S}
, denoted by
U,V,\dots
. We consider terms generated by the following context free grammar, where
A,B\in\mathcal{S}
and
s\in\Sigma
:

\begin{array}[]{rcccccccccccccccc}c&::=&{id}_{A}&\mid&{id}_{1}&\mid&s&\mid&\sigma^{\otimes}_{A,B}&\mid&c;c&\mid&c\otimes c\end{array}

The rules in Table
1
assigns a type
U\to V
to terms. Well-typed terms, taken modulo the axioms in the same table, are the arrows of
(\mathbf{Diag}_{\Sigma},\otimes,1)
, the strict symmetric monoidal category freely generated by
\Sigma
. Its objects are words in
\mathcal{S}^{*}
. Arrows of
\mathbf{Diag}_{\Sigma}
admit a graphical representation in terms of
string diagrams

[
46
,
65
]
. The grammar above can be depicted diagrammatically as follows:

c

\Coloneqq

A
A

\,\mid\,

\,\mid\,

B
A
s

\,\mid\,

B
A
B
A

\,\mid\,

V
U
c
c

\,\mid\,

V
U
c
V^{\prime}
U^{\prime}
c

\,\mid\,

The diagrammatic notation internalises the axioms in Table
1
, yielding proofs that are both more concise and more intuitive. Throughout the paper, we will also rely on the term-based notation, which is often more succinct for inductive definitions.

A
monoidal theory

\mathbb{T}=(\Sigma,E)
consists of a monoidal signature
\Sigma
and a set
E
of pairs of arrows of
\mathbf{Diag}_{\Sigma}
of the same type. Let
=_{\mathbb{T}}
be the congruence closure (w.r.t.
;
and
\otimes
) of
E
. We write
\mathbf{Diag}_{\mathbb{T}}
for the monoidal category obtained as the quotient of
\mathbf{Diag}_{\Sigma}
by
=_{\mathbb{T}}
and
Q_{\mathbb{T}}\colon\mathbf{Diag}_{\Sigma}\to\mathbf{Diag}_{\mathbb{T}}
for the monoidal functor mapping each diagram into its
=_{\mathbb{T}}
equivalence class.

\begin{array}[]{c}\hline\cr\hline\cr\begin{array}[]{c}\begin{array}[]{ccc}{id_{1}\colon 1\to 1}&{id_{A}\colon A\to A}&{\sigma_{A,B}^{\otimes}\colon A\otimes B\to B\otimes A}\\[3.00003pt]
\frac{\mathit{ar}(s)=U\hskip 8.19447pt\mathit{coar}(s)=V}{s\colon U\to V}&\frac{c\colon U\to Vd\colon V\to W}{c;d\colon U\to W}&\frac{c\colon U_{1}\to V_{1}d\colon U_{2}\to V_{2}}{c\otimes d\colon U_{1}\otimes U_{2}\to V_{1}\otimes V_{2}}\end{array}\end{array}\\[5.0pt]
\begin{array}[]{cc}\hline\cr\begin{array}[]{c}(c;d);e=c;(d;e)\qquad id_{U};c=c=c;id_{Q}\\
(c_{1}\otimes c_{2});(d_{1}\otimes d_{2})=(c_{1};d_{1})\otimes(c_{2};d_{2})\end{array}&\begin{array}[]{c}id_{1}\otimes c=c=c\otimes id_{1}\qquad(c\otimes d)\,\otimes e=c\otimes\,(d\otimes e)\\
\sigma_{U,V};\sigma_{V,U}=id_{U\otimes V}\qquad(s\otimes id_{W});\sigma_{V,W}=\sigma_{U,W};(id_{W}\otimes s)\end{array}\end{array}\\
\hline\cr\hline\cr\end{array}

Typing rules (top) and axioms (bottom) for freely generated strict symmetric monoidal categories.

Arities and coarities are determined by the number of ports on the left and on the right: for instance,
has arity
A^{2}=AA
and coarity
A
, while
has arity
A
and coarity
A^{0}=1
.

The first three generators of
B
correspond to the operations and constants of Boolean algebras, namely
\wedge
,
\neg
, and
1
.
The generator
copy
, denoted by
, takes a Boolean signal as input and produces two identical outputs.
The generator
discard
, denoted by
, takes a Boolean signal as input and discards it.
To make this formal, we interpret each generator
s\in B
with arity
A^{n}
and coarity
A^{m}
as function
\langle\!\langle{s}\rangle\!\rangle_{\!\footnotesize{B}}\colon 2^{n}\to 2^{m}
where
2
is the set of Booleans
\{0,1\}
and
2^{0}
is the singleton set
1\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}\{\bullet\}
.

(1)

Such interpretation gives rise to a symmetric monoidal functor
\langle\!\langle{-}\rangle\!\rangle_{\!\footnotesize{B}}
from
(\mathbf{Diag}_{B},\otimes,1)
to
(\mathbf{Set},\otimes,1)
. The latter is the category of sets and functions where the monoidal tensor is simply cartesian product.
The functor
\langle\!\langle{-}\rangle\!\rangle_{\!\footnotesize{B}}\colon(\mathbf{Diag}_{B},\otimes,1)\to(\mathbf{Set},\otimes,1)
is defined on objects as
\langle\!\langle{A^{n}}\rangle\!\rangle_{\!\footnotesize{B}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}2^{n}
and on arrows as

\langle\!\langle{{id}_{A}}\rangle\!\rangle_{\!\footnotesize{B}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}{id}_{2}\;\;\langle\!\langle{{id}_{1}}\rangle\!\rangle_{\!\footnotesize{B}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}{id}_{1}\;\;\langle\!\langle{\sigma^{\otimes}_{A,A}}\rangle\!\rangle_{\!\footnotesize{B}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}\sigma^{\otimes}_{2,2}\;\;\langle\!\langle{c;d}\rangle\!\rangle_{\!\footnotesize{B}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}\langle\!\langle{c}\rangle\!\rangle_{\!\footnotesize{B}};\langle\!\langle{d}\rangle\!\rangle_{\!\footnotesize{B}}\;\;\langle\!\langle{c\otimes d}\rangle\!\rangle_{\!\footnotesize{B}}=\langle\!\langle{c}\rangle\!\rangle_{\!\footnotesize{B}}\otimes\langle\!\langle{d}\rangle\!\rangle_{\!\footnotesize{B}}

(2)

We regard diagrams as syntax and
\langle\!\langle{-}\rangle\!\rangle_{\!\footnotesize{B}}
as the map assigning semantics to syntax. Semantic equality–i.e., the congruence induced by
\langle\!\langle{-}\rangle\!\rangle_{\!\footnotesize{B}}
– is axiomatised by the laws in Figure
1
.
The equalities in the first block are the standard axioms of Boolean algebras, where
the constant
0
and the
or
gate
are defined as expected (see Figure
2
).
Note that, in the string-diagrammatic setting, the structural maps
and
must be made explicit, for instance in (
1
) that is the usual law of non contradiction.
The equalities in the second block state that
and
form a commutative comonoid.
The equalities in the third and fourth blocks impose naturality of
and
, respectively.

We write
\mathbb{B}
for the monoidal theory consisting of the signature
B
and the axioms in Figure
1
.

Theorem 1

(From
[
59
]
)
.

For all

Figure 1
:
The monoidal theory of Boolean algebras.

We conclude this section by fixing some syntactic sugar, collected in Figure
2
.
The
xnor
gate
takes two inputs and outputs
1
if they are equal and
0
otherwise.
The
multiplexer

takes three inputs and returns one output: if the first input is
1
, then it outputs the second input, otherwise the third input.
The
m
-ary multiplexer
m
m
m
works similarly, but it takes
2m+1
inputs: if the first input is
1
, then it outputs the first
m
inputs, otherwise it outputs the second
m
inputs.
Figure
2
also defines
m
-ary discard
m
and copier
m
. Note that, for the sake of readability of string diagrams, we label wires by some natural number
n
as an abbreviation for
A^{n}
.

Intuitively,
is the dual of
: it compares two inputs and, if these are equal, it outputs that value; otherwise, it produces no output. Thus,
does not denote a function but a
partial function

Let
(\mathbf{Par},\otimes,1)
be the category of sets and partial functions, where
\otimes
is the cartesian product of sets and, for all partial functions
f_{1}\colon X_{1}\to Y_{1}
and
f_{2}\colon X_{2}\to Y_{2}
,
f_{1}\otimes f_{2}\colon X_{1}\times X_{2}\to Y_{1}\times Y_{2}
is defined for all
(x_{1},x_{2})\in X_{1}\times X_{2}
as

f_{1}\otimes f_{2}(x_{1},x_{2})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}\begin{cases}(\,f_{1}(x_{1}),\,f_{2}(x_{2})\,)&\text{ if }f_{1}(x_{1})\neq\bot\text{, }f_{2}(x_{2})\neq\bot\\
\bot&\text{ otherwise}\end{cases}

(3)

Above and in the rest of the paper, we write
f(x)=\bot
to say that
f
is undefined on
x
.
The obvious injection
P\colon(\mathbf{Set},\otimes,1)\to(\mathbf{Par},\otimes,1)
is easily proved to be a symmetric monoidal functor.

The strategy for proving completeness is as follows.
First, we show that any diagram
c
in
\mathbf{Diag}_{PB}
can be decomposed into two Boolean circuits
D_{c}
and
T_{c}
in
\mathbf{Diag}_{B}
(Proposition
6
).
We then appeal to the completeness result for Boolean circuits (Theorem
1
).

Definition 5
.

c\in\mathbf{Diag}_{PB}[A^{n},A^{m}]

D_{c}\in\mathbf{Diag}_{B}[A^{n},A]

T_{c}\in\mathbf{Diag}_{B}[A^{n},A^{m}]

(6)

Intuitively,
D_{c}
and
T_{c}
represent, respectively, the domain and the total component of
c
.
The diagram
D_{c}
returns
1
if the input of
c
lies in the domain of definition of
c
, and
0
otherwise.
The diagram
T_{c}
returns the output of
c
when the input lies in its domain, and a vector of
0
otherwise.
For instance, the domain of
is the
\mathrm{xnor}
gate: it returns
1
if and only if the two inputs are equal.
Its total part is given by the
\wedge
gate: it returns
1
precisely when both inputs are
1
.
Similarly, the domain of
c\otimes d
is given by the conjunction of the domains of
c
and
d
.
Its total part returns the total parts of
c
and
d
when the domain evaluates to
1
, and
0
otherwise.

Lemma 8
.

For all
b\in\mathbf{Diag}_{B}[1,A^{n}]
and
c,d\in\mathbf{Diag}_{PB}[A^{n},A^{m}]
,

if
\langle\!\langle{b;c}\rangle\!\rangle_{PB}=\langle\!\langle{b;d}\rangle\!\rangle_{PB}
, then
\langle\!\langle{b;D_{c}}\rangle\!\rangle_{PB}=\langle\!\langle{b;D_{d}}\rangle\!\rangle_{PB}
and
\langle\!\langle{b;T_{c}}\rangle\!\rangle_{PB}=\langle\!\langle{b;T_{d}}\rangle\!\rangle_{PB}
.

Theorem 9

(Completeness)
.

For all
c,d\in\mathbf{Diag}_{PB}[A^{n},A^{m}]
, if
\langle\!\langle{c}\rangle\!\rangle_{PB}=\langle\!\langle{d}\rangle\!\rangle_{PB}
then
c=_{\mathbb{PB}}d
.

Proof.

For all
b\in\mathbf{Diag}_{B}[1,A^{n}]
, functoriality of
\langle\!\langle{-}\rangle\!\rangle_{PB}
and the hypothesis entail that

\langle\!\langle{b;c}\rangle\!\rangle_{PB}=\langle\!\langle{b}\rangle\!\rangle_{PB};\langle\!\langle{c}\rangle\!\rangle_{PB}=\langle\!\langle{b}\rangle\!\rangle_{PB};\langle\!\langle{d}\rangle\!\rangle_{PB}=\langle\!\langle{b;d}\rangle\!\rangle_{PB}\text{.}

By Lemma
8
,
\langle\!\langle{b;D_{c}}\rangle\!\rangle_{PB}=\langle\!\langle{b;D_{d}}\rangle\!\rangle_{PB}
and
\langle\!\langle{b;T_{c}}\rangle\!\rangle_{PB}=\langle\!\langle{b;T_{d}}\rangle\!\rangle_{PB}
for all
b\in\mathbf{Diag}_{B}[1,A^{n}]
. Hence
\langle\!\langle{D_{c}}\rangle\!\rangle_{PB}=\langle\!\langle{D_{d}}\rangle\!\rangle_{PB}
and
\langle\!\langle{T_{c}}\rangle\!\rangle_{PB}=\langle\!\langle{T_{d}}\rangle\!\rangle_{PB}
. Now, since
D_{c},D_{d},T_{c}
and
T_{d}
are Boolean circuits in
\mathbf{Diag}_{B}
, then by Theorem
1
it holds that
D_{c}=_{\mathbb{B}}D_{d}
and
T_{c}=_{\mathbb{B}}T_{d}
. Finally, by Proposition
6
, since
c
and
d
decompose through the same domain and total part, we have that
c=_{\scalebox{0.6}{$\mathbb{PB}$}}d
.
∎

Moreover, one can characterise exactly the image of
\mathbf{Diag}_{PB}
through
\langle\!\langle{-}\rangle\!\rangle_{PB}
. Let
\mathbf{Par}_{2}
be the full subcategory of
\mathbf{Par}
where objects are powers of the set
2
, i.e.,
2^{n}
for all
n\in\mathbb{N}
.

Proposition 10
.

The functor
\langle\!\langle{-}\rangle\!\rangle_{PB}\colon\mathbf{Diag}_{{PB}}\to\mathbf{Par}
factors as

\textstyle{\mathbf{Diag}_{PB}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{Q_{\mathbb{PB}}}
\textstyle{\mathbf{Diag}_{\mathbb{PB}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\cong}
\textstyle{\mathbf{Par}_{2}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\textstyle{\mathbf{Par}}

where the rightmost functors is the obvious injections and the central arrow is an isomorphism.

. The gate
p
outputs a Boolean value, which is
1
with probability
p
and
0
with probability
1-p
.

To provide a formal semantics, it is convenient to recall some key notions. We write
\mathcal{D}_{\leq}(X)
for the set of all (finitely supported probability)
subdistributions
over a set
X
, namely, functions
d\colon X\to[0,1]
such that
\sum_{x\in X}d(x)\leq 1
, and
d(x)\neq 0
for finitely many
x\in X
. For all
x\in X
, we write
\delta_{x}\in\mathcal{D}_{\leq}(X)
for the Dirac distribution at
x
;
\star\in\mathcal{D}_{\leq}(X)
for the null subdistribution:
\star(x)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}0
for all
x\in X
; for all
p\in(0,1)
and
d_{1},d_{2}\in\mathcal{D}_{\leq}(X)
, we write
d_{1}+_{p}d_{2}
for the subdistributions mapping each
x\in X
into
p\cdot d_{1}(x)+(1-p)\cdot d_{2}(x)
.

The assignment
X\mapsto\mathcal{D}_{\leq}(X)
extends to a monad
\mathcal{D}_{\leq}\colon\mathbf{Set}\to\mathbf{Set}
(see e.g.,
[
40
]
). Its Kleisli category is denoted by
\mathcal{KL}(\mathcal{D}_{\leq})
:
objects are sets; morphisms
f\colon X\to Y
are functions
X\to\mathcal{D}_{\leq}(Y)
.
We often write
f(y\mid x)
for
f(x)(y)
, as this number represents the probability that
f
returns
y
given the input
x
.
Identities
{id}_{X}\colon X\to\mathcal{D}_{\leq}(X)
map each
x\in X
to
\delta_{x}
.
For two functions
f\colon X\to\mathcal{D}_{\leq}(Y)
and
g\colon Y\to\mathcal{D}_{\leq}(Z)
, their composition in
\mathcal{KL}(\mathcal{D}_{\leq})
is defined as
f;g(z\mid x)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}\sum_{y\in Y}f(y\mid x)\cdot g(z\mid y)
.

This category carries a symmetric monoidal structure

(\mathcal{KL}(\mathcal{D}_{\leq}),\otimes,1)
, where
\otimes
is the cartesian product of sets and, for arrows
f\colon X_{1}\to Y_{1}
and
g\colon X_{2}\to Y_{2}
,
f\otimes g\colon X_{1}\times X_{2}\to Y_{1}\times Y_{2}
is defined as

\displaystyle f\otimes g((y_{1},y_{2})\mid(x_{1},x_{2}))

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}f(y_{1}\mid x_{1})\cdot g(y_{2}\mid x_{2})\text{.}

(7)

Finally, the symmetric monoidal functor
J\colon(\mathbf{Par},\otimes,1)\to(\mathcal{KL}(\mathcal{D}_{\leq}),\otimes,1)
is the identity on objects and associates to a partial function
f\colon X\to Y
the function
J(f)\colon X\to\mathcal{D}_{\leq}(Y)
, mapping
x
to
\delta_{f(x)}
, if
f(x)
is defined and to the null distribution
\star
otherwise.

A natural goal, mirroring the case of (partial) Boolean circuits, is to obtain a complete axiomatisation of semantic equality. Instead, we establish a complete axiomatisation for probabilistic Boolean tapes, a formalism into which circuits can be encoded.

5
From circuits to tapes

Example 30 in
[
8
]
encodes probabilistic Boolean circuits as
probabilistic Boolean tapes
.
This relies on
\mathcal{KL}(\mathcal{D}_{\leq})
having finite coproducts, which induce a second monoidal structure
(\mathcal{KL}(\mathcal{D}_{\leq}),\oplus,0)
, where
\oplus
is disjoint union of sets with units
0\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}\{\}
;
for
f\colon X_{1}\to Y_{1}
and
g\colon X_{2}\to Y_{2}
, the arrow
f\oplus g\colon X_{1}\oplus X_{2}\to Y_{1}\oplus Y_{2}
is defined, for all
u\in X_{1}\oplus X_{2}
,
v\in Y_{1}\oplus Y_{2}
, by

\displaystyle f\oplus g(v\mid u)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}\begin{cases}f(y_{1}\mid x_{1})&\text{if }u=\iota_{1}(x_{1})\text{ and }v=\iota_{1}(y_{1}),\\
g(y_{2}\mid x_{2})&\text{if }u=\iota_{2}(x_{2})\text{ and }v=\iota_{2}(y_{2}),\\
0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

(9)

Here
\iota_{1}
and
\iota_{2}
are the coproduct injections. In
\mathcal{KL}(\mathcal{D}_{\leq})
,
\otimes
distributes over
\oplus
, so
(\mathcal{KL}(\mathcal{D}_{\leq}),\oplus,\otimes,0,1)
forms a
rig category
, aka bimonoidal category
[
49
]
. Moreover, for each object
X
, the arrows

\begin{array}[]{cccc}\begin{array}[]{rcl}{}^{p}\!\!\lhd_{X}\colon X&\to&X\oplus X\\
x&\mapsto&\delta_{\iota_{1}(x)}+_{p}\delta_{\iota_{2}(x)}\end{array}&\begin{array}[]{rcl}\rotatebox{90.0}{$\multimapinv$}_{X}\colon X&\to&0\\
x&\mapsto&\star\end{array}&\begin{array}[]{rcl}\rotatebox{90.0}{$\multimap$}_{X}\colon 0&\to&X\\
\text{ }\end{array}&\begin{array}[]{rcl}\rhd_{X}\colon X\oplus X&\to&X\\
\iota_{i}(x)&\mapsto&\delta_{x}\end{array}\end{array}

(10)

are central:
(\rhd_{X},\rotatebox{90.0}{$\multimap$}_{X})
and
(^{p}\!\!\lhd_{X},\rotatebox{90.0}{$\multimapinv$}_{X})
form, respectively, a natural and coherent
monoid
and
co-pointed convex algebra
, namely they satisfy the laws in Tables
3(d)
and
3(e)
in Appendix
A
.

These structures are exploited in
\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{PB})
, the category of probabilistic Boolean tapes. Consider the following context-free grammar, where
p\in(0,1)
,
U,V\in\mathcal{S}^{*}
, and
c
is an arrow in
\mathbf{Diag}_{PB}
:

\begin{array}[]{rcccccccccccccccccccc}\mathfrak{t}&::=&{}^{p}\!\!\lhd_{U}&\mid&\!\rotatebox{90.0}{$\multimapinv$}_{U}&\mid&\underline{\smash{\overline{\;c\vphantom{t}\;}}}&\mid&\rotatebox{90.0}{$\multimap$}_{U}&\mid&\rhd_{U}&\mid&{id}_{U}&\mid&{id}_{0}&\mid&\sigma_{U,V}^{\oplus}&\mid&\mathfrak{t};\mathfrak{t}&\mid&\mathfrak{t}\oplus\mathfrak{t}\end{array}

(11)

We restrict to terms typable by the rules of Table
3(a)
. Types are arrows
P\to Q
, where
P,Q\in(\mathcal{S}^{*})^{*}
are viewed as sums
\bigoplus_{i=1}^{n}{U}_{i}
, with each
U_{i}=\bigotimes_{j=1}^{m_{i}}{A}
.

The category
\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{PB})
has as set of objects
(\mathcal{S}^{*})^{*}
. Arrows in
\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{PB})[P,Q]
are terms of type
P\to Q
modulo the axioms in Table
3
, i.e., those of natural and coherent monoids, co-pcas and strict symmetric monoidal categories. By the latter axioms,
(\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{PB}),\oplus,0)
is a symmetric monoidal category.
Define
P\otimes Q\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}\bigoplus_{i}{\bigoplus_{j}{U_{i}V_{j}}}
for
P=\bigoplus_{i}{U_{i}}
and
Q=\bigoplus_{j}{V_{j}}
; together with definition of
\mathfrak{t}_{1}\otimes\mathfrak{t}_{2}
in Table
4
in Appendix
A
, this yields another symmetric monoidal structure
(\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{PB}),\otimes,1)
, which makes
(\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{PB}),\oplus,\otimes,0,1)
a rig category. Crucially, there is a morphism of rig categories
\left\llbracket-\right\rrbracket\colon\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{PB})\to\mathcal{KL}(\mathcal{D}_{\leq})
assigning to each tape its semantics in
\mathcal{KL}(\mathcal{D}_{\leq})
:

\left\llbracket{}^{p}\!\!\lhd_{A^{n}}\right\rrbracket\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}\;^{p}\!\!\lhd_{2^{n}}

\left\llbracket\rotatebox{90.0}{$\multimapinv$}_{A^{n}}\right\rrbracket\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}\rotatebox{90.0}{$\multimapinv$}_{2^{n}}

\left\llbracket\,\underline{\smash{\overline{\;c\vphantom{t}\;}}}\,\right\rrbracket\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}J(\langle\!\langle{c}\rangle\!\rangle_{PB})

\left\llbracket\rotatebox{90.0}{$\multimap$}_{A^{n}}\right\rrbracket\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}\rotatebox{90.0}{$\multimap$}_{2^{n}}

\left\llbracket\rhd_{A^{n}}\right\rrbracket\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}\rhd_{2^{n}}

\left\llbracket{id}_{A^{n}}\right\rrbracket\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}{id}_{2^{n}}

\left\llbracket{id}_{0}\right\rrbracket\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}{id}_{0}

\left\llbracket\sigma^{\oplus}_{A^{n},A^{m}}\right\rrbracket\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}\sigma^{\oplus}_{2^{n},2^{m}}

\left\llbracket\mathfrak{s};\mathfrak{t}\right\rrbracket\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}\left\llbracket\mathfrak{s}\right\rrbracket;\left\llbracket\mathfrak{t}\right\rrbracket

\left\llbracket\mathfrak{s}\oplus\mathfrak{t}\right\rrbracket\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}\left\llbracket\mathfrak{s}\right\rrbracket\oplus\left\llbracket\mathfrak{t}\right\rrbracket

(12)

have a diagrammatic representation. The grammar in (

) is depicted as

The encoding
\mathcal{E}(-)\colon(\mathbf{Diag}_{PrB},\otimes,1)\to(\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{PB}),\otimes,1)

Proposition 12
.

For all
c\in\mathbf{Diag}_{PrB}
,
\langle\!\langle{c}\rangle\!\rangle=\left\llbracket\mathcal{E}(c)\right\rrbracket
.

The above result asserts that the encoding
\mathcal{E}(-)
preserves the semantics. Thus, instead of axiomatising the equivalence induced by the semantics on probabilistic Boolean circuits, we rather axiomatise the one on tapes (Corollary
29
) and then check equivalence of circuits by encoding them into tapes (Corollary
30
). Before illustrating the axiomatision for tapes and prove its completeness in Section
7
, we recall some key results from
[
6
]
in the next section. We concluse this section by recalling from
[
8
]
an example comparing the expressivity of circuits and tapes.

6
On Freely Generated Convex Biproduct Categories

The category
\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{PB})
of probabilistic Boolean tapes is an instance of a general construction, introduced in
[
7
]
, which associates to any category
\mathbf{C}
a category
\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{C})
.
The latter is defined analogously to
\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{PB})
, but with
\mathcal{S}^{*}
replaced by
Ob(\mathbf{C})
and arrows of
\mathbf{Diag}_{PB}
replaced by arrows of
\mathbf{C}
. Consequently, the objects of
\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{C})
are elements of
Ob(\mathbf{C})^{*}
, and its arrows are equivalence classes of well-typed terms generated by the grammar in (
11
), where now
U,V\in Ob(\mathbf{C})
and
c
ranges over arrows of
\mathbf{C}
.

In this section, we briefly recall from
[
7
]
the properties of
\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{C})
that are needed for the completeness proof.
Throughout, all categories are tacitly assumed to be locally small, and
\mathbf{Cat}
denotes the category of locally small categories.

6.1
PCA-enriched categories

Recall from
[
68
,
14
]
that a
pointed convex algebra
(pca) consists of a set
X
, a designated element
\star\in X
and, for all
p
in the open real interval
(0,1)
, a function
+_{p}\colon X\times X\to X
such that, by fixing
\tilde{p}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}pq
and
\tilde{q}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}\frac{p(1-q)}{1-pq}
, the following laws hold for all
x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}\in X
.

(x_{1}+_{q}x_{2})+_{p}x_{3}=x_{1}+_{\tilde{p}}(x_{2}+_{\tilde{q}}x_{3})\qquad x_{1}+_{p}x_{2}=x_{2}+_{1-p}x_{1}\qquad x_{1}+_{p}x_{1}=x_{1}

(14)

We denote by
\mathbf{PCA}
the category of pcas and their morphisms, i.e., functions preserving
\star
and
+_{p}
.

In any pca,
+_{p}
is easily extended to any
p\in[0,1]
by fixing
x+_{1}y\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}x
and
x+_{0}y\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}y
.
This can be further extended for any
n\in\mathbb{N}
and
p_{1},\dots,p_{n}\in[0,1]
inductively as

\sum_{i=1}^{0}p_{i}\cdot(-)_{i}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}\star
and
\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}p_{i}\cdot(-)_{i}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}(-)_{1}+_{p_{1}}\sum_{j=1}^{n}q_{j}\cdot(-)_{j}

where
(-)_{j}=(-)_{i+1}
and
q_{j}
is
\frac{p_{i+1}}{1-p_{1}}
if
p_{1}\neq 1
and
0
otherwise. For
n=1
, this is the
multiplication by a scalar

p\in[0,1]
, shortly defined as
p\cdot x\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}x+_{p}\star
.

The archetypical example of a pca is
\mathcal{D}_{\leq}(X)
with
+_{p}
and
\star
defined as in Section
4
. Such pca enjoys an additional property called cancellativity. A pca
(X,+_{p},\star)
is
cancellative
(or, in the terminology of
[
66
]
, cancellative at
\star
) if for all
x,y\in X
and
p\in(0,1)
:

p\cdot x=p\cdot y\Rightarrow x=y
.

A category
\mathbf{C}
is
\mathbf{PCA}
-enriched
if every homset carries a pca structure and composition of arrows is a pcas morphism, namely that the following equalities hold for all properly typed arrows
e,f,g,h
.

e;(f+_{p}g)=(e;f)+_{p}(e;g)\qquad(f+_{p}g);h=(f;h+_{p}g;h)\qquad f;\star=\star=\star;f

(15)

A functor
F
is
\mathbf{PCA}
-enriched if it preserves the pca structure of each homset.
\mathbf{PCA}
-enriched categories and functors form a category, denoted by
\mathbf{PCACat}
.

Moreover, a monoidal category
(\mathbf{C},\otimes,1)
is
monoidally enriched
over
\mathbf{PCA}
if the following holds.

e\otimes(f+_{p}g)=(e\otimes f)+_{p}(e\otimes g)\qquad(f+_{p}g)\otimes h=(f\otimes h)+_{p}(g\otimes h)\qquad\star\otimes\,f=\star=f\otimes\star

(16)

The category
\mathcal{KL}(\mathcal{D}_{\leq})
is monoidally enriched over
\mathbf{PCA}
: for all
f,g\colon X\to Y
,
x\in X
,
y\in Y
and
p\in(0,1)
,

f+_{p}g(y|x)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}p\cdot f(y|x)+(1-p)\cdot g(y|x)
and
\star_{X,Y}(y|x)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}0
.
Also
\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{C})
is
\mathbf{PCA}
-enriched:
f+_{p}g\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}\,^{p}\!\!\lhd_{X};(f\oplus g);\rhd_{Y}
and
\star_{X,Y}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}\rotatebox{90.0}{$\multimapinv$}_{X};\rotatebox{90.0}{$\multimap$}_{Y}
.
Such enrichment is monoidal whenever
(\mathbf{C},\otimes,1)
is a symmetric monoidal category: see
[
8
, Thm. 27]
.

6.2
Convex Biproduct Categories

We now recall the definition of convex biproduct categories from
[
7
]
, which are suitable
\mathbf{PCA}
-enriched categories where coproducts enjoy an additional universal property, similar to the one of products.

Definition 14
.

Let
X_{1}
,
X_{2}
be two objects of a
\mathbf{PCA}
-enriched category
\mathbf{C}
. The
convex product
of
X_{1}
and
X_{2}
is an object
Z
with two arrows
\pi_{1}\colon Z\to X_{1}
and
\pi_{2}\colon Z\to X_{2}
satisfying the following property: for all
p_{1},p_{2}\in[0,1]
such that
p_{1}+p_{2}\leq 1
and all arrows
f_{1}\colon A\to X_{1}
,
f_{2}\colon A\to X_{2}
, there exists a unique arrow
h\colon A\to Z
such that
h;\pi_{1}=p_{1}\cdot f
and
h;\pi_{2}=p_{2}\cdot g
.

Similarly, the convex product of
n
objects
X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}
is an object
Z
with arrows
\pi_{i}\colon Z\to X_{i}
for
i=1,\ldots,n
satisfying the following property: for all
p_{1},\dots,p_{n}\in[0,1]
where
\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}\leq 1
and arrows
f_{i}\colon A\to X_{i}
, there exists a unique arrow
h\colon A\to Z
such that
h;\pi_{i}=p_{i}\cdot f_{i}
for all
i=1,\ldots,n
. Observe that, by definition, the 0-ary convex product is a final object. Hereafter, we will denote the unique arrow
h
by
\langle f_{1},\dots,f_{n}\rangle_{\vec{p}}
where
\vec{p}
is a compact notation for
p_{1},\dots,p_{n}
.

Definition 15
.

A
convex biproduct category
is a
\mathbf{PCA}
-enriched category
\mathbf{C}
with an object
0
which is both initial and final and, for every pair of objects
X_{1},X_{2}
, an object
X_{1}\oplus X_{2}
and morphisms
\pi_{i}\colon X_{1}\oplus X_{2}\to X_{i}
and
\iota_{i}\colon X_{i}\to X_{1}\oplus X_{2}
such that
(X_{1}\oplus X_{2},\iota_{1},\iota_{2})
is a coproduct,
(X_{1}\oplus X_{2},\pi_{1},\pi_{2})
is a convex product and
\iota_{i};\pi_{j}={id}_{X_{i}}
if
i=j
and
\iota_{i};\pi_{j}=\star_{X_{i},X_{j}}
if
i\neq j
.

A morphism of convex biproduct categories is a
\mathbf{PCA}
-enriched functor
F\colon\mathbf{C}\to\mathbf{D}
preserving finite coproducts. We write
\mathbf{CBCat}
for the category of convex biproduct categories and their morphisms.

Note that the above definition is obtained from that of
category with finite biproducts

[
51
,
20
]
by just replacing products by convex products. Examples of convex biproduct categories include
\mathcal{KL}(\mathcal{D}_{\leq})
, its continuous analogue (see
[
7
]
) and, most importantly,
\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{C})
.

Theorem 16
.

\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{C})
is a convex biproduct category. In particular, for every arrow
\mathfrak{t}\colon U\to\bigoplus_{i=1}^{n}U_{i}
in
\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{C})
, there exist
n
arrows
\mathfrak{t}_{i}\colon U\to U_{i}
such that
\mathfrak{t}=\langle\mathfrak{t}_{1},\dots\mathfrak{t}_{n}\rangle_{\vec{p}}
for some
\vec{p}=p_{1},\dots,p_{n}
.

Crucially, the assignment
\mathbf{C}\mapsto\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{C})
extends to a functor
\mathbf{T}(-)\colon\mathbf{Cat}\to\mathbf{CBCat}
which is left adjoint to the forgetful functor
U\colon\mathbf{CBCat}\to\mathbf{Cat}
.

Theorem 17
.

\mathbf{T}(-)\colon\mathbf{Cat}\to\mathbf{CBCat}
is left adjoint to
U\colon\mathbf{CBCat}\to\mathbf{Cat}
.

In other words,
\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{C})
is the convex biproduct category freely generated by
\mathbf{C}
. Theorems 1 and 2 in
[
6
]
illustrate that such adjunction is decomposed in the following two adjunctions, where
\mathbf{PCACat}
denotes the category of
\mathbf{PCA}
-enriched categories and
\mathbf{PCA}
-enriched functors:

\textstyle{\mathbf{Cat}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{(-)^{+}}
\textstyle{\;\;{\tiny{\bot}}}
\textstyle{\mathbf{PCACat}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{U}
\scriptstyle{\mathbf{StMat}(-)}
\textstyle{\;{\tiny{\bot}}}
\textstyle{\mathbf{CBCat}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{U}

(17)

Corollary 18
.

For all categories
\mathbf{C}
,
\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{C})
is isomorphic to
\mathbf{StMat}(\mathbf{C}^{+})
in
\mathbf{CBCat}
.

While it is not strictly necessary for our completeness proof, it is useful to provide some intuition about the two constructions in (
17
).

The leftmost adjunction is an instance of a general result about enriching over arbitrary algebraic theories: see
[
16
, Prop. 6.4.7]
or
[
69
, Cor. 1]
. For every category
\mathbf{C}
one obtains
\mathbf{PCA}
-enriched category
\mathbf{C}^{+}
: objects of
\mathbf{C}^{+}
are those of
\mathbf{C}
; for all objects
X,Y
, the homset is defined as
\mathbf{C}^{+}[X,Y]\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}\mathcal{D}_{\leq}(\mathbf{C}[X,Y])
. For
d_{1}\colon X\to Y
and
d_{2}\colon Y\to Z
, their composition
d_{1};d_{2}\colon X\to Z
is defined for all
h\in\mathbf{C}[X,Z]
as
d_{1};d_{2}(h)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}\sum_{\{(f,g)\mid f;g=h\}}d_{1}(f)\cdot d_{2}(g)
; The identity
{id}_{X}\colon X\to X
is given by
\delta_{id_{X}}
.

The second adjunction is an adaptation of
[
51
, Exercises VIII.2.5-6]
which constructs a category of matrices from a category enriched over commutative monoids.
Given a
\mathbf{PCA}
-enriched category
\mathbf{C}
,
\mathbf{StMat}(\mathbf{C})
is the category of
stochastic matrices
over
\mathbf{C}
.
In a nutshell, objects of
\mathbf{StMat}(\mathbf{C})
are words in
Ob(\mathbf{C})^{*}
, while arrows
M\colon\bigoplus_{k=1}^{n}U_{k}\to\bigoplus_{k=1}^{m}V_{k}
are matrices with
(j,i)
-entries given by pairs
(p_{ji},f_{ji})
where
f_{ji}\in\mathbf{C}[U_{i},V_{j}]
and
p_{ji}\in[0,1]
satisfy
\sum_{j=1}^{m}p_{ji}\leq 1
. The composition of two morphisms is given by matrix multiplication where addition is given by the pca enrichment of
\mathbf{C}
and multiplication by composition of arrows in
\mathbf{C}
.

Figure 5
:
Axioms for tapes of partial Boolean circuits.

7.1
Axiomatisation

To obtain a complete axiomatisation, we need to add to
\mathbb{PB}
the axioms in Figure
5
.

First, the axiom (
5
) forces the equality of
\bot
and

. Then, consider the tape diagram on the right-hand side of (
5
): with probability
\frac{1}{2}
it tests if the input is
1
and returns
1
and, with probability
\frac{1}{2}
, tests if the input is
0
and returns
0
. The equality (
5
) forces such tape to be equal to
\frac{1}{2}\cdot{id}_{A}
. Finally, axiom (
5
) is an implication which asserts cancellativity: see Section
6.1
.

From the theory
\mathbb{PB}
together with the axioms in Figure
5
, we generate a congruence
\dot{\sim}
on
\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{PB})
via the inference rules below.

\centering\begin{array}[]{c}\begin{array}[]{c@{\qquad\qquad}c@{\qquad\qquad}c@{\qquad\qquad}c@{\qquad\qquad}c}\frac{\mathfrak{t}_{1}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\eqref{ax:AXPBP2}}}{{=}}\mathfrak{t}_{2}}{\mathfrak{t}_{1}\dot{\sim}\mathfrak{t}_{2}}\quad\textsc{right=\eqref{ax:AXPBP2}}&\frac{\mathfrak{t}_{1}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\eqref{ax:AXPBP1}}}{{=}}\mathfrak{t}_{2}}{\mathfrak{t}_{1}\dot{\sim}\mathfrak{t}_{2}}\quad\textsc{right=\eqref{ax:AXPBP1}}&\frac{-}{\mathfrak{t}\dot{\sim}\mathfrak{t}}\quad\textsc{right=($\textsc{R}$)}&\frac{\mathfrak{t}_{1}\dot{\sim}\mathfrak{t}_{2}}{\mathfrak{t}_{2}\dot{\sim}\mathfrak{t}_{1}}\quad\textsc{right=($\textsc{S}$)}&\frac{\mathfrak{t}_{1}\dot{\sim}\mathfrak{t}_{2}\hskip 8.19447pt\mathfrak{t}_{2}\dot{\sim}\mathfrak{t}_{3}}{\mathfrak{t}_{1}\dot{\sim}\mathfrak{t}_{3}}\quad\textsc{right=($\textsc{T}$)}\end{array}\\[10.0pt]
\begin{array}[]{c@{\qquad}c@{\qquad}c@{\qquad}c@{\qquad}c}\frac{c=_{\scalebox{0.6}{$\mathbb{PB}$}}d}{\overline{\underline{\;c\vphantom{d_{A}}\;}}\dot{\sim}\overline{\underline{\;d\vphantom{d_{A}}\;}}}\quad\textsc{right=($\mathbb{PB}$)}&\frac{p\cdot\mathfrak{t}\dot{\sim}p\cdot\mathfrak{s}}{\mathfrak{t}\dot{\sim}\mathfrak{s}}\quad\textsc{right=\eqref{ax:canc}}&\frac{\mathfrak{t}_{1}\dot{\sim}\mathfrak{t}_{2}\hskip 8.19447pt\mathfrak{s}_{1}\dot{\sim}\mathfrak{s}_{2}}{\mathfrak{t}_{1};\mathfrak{s}_{1}\dot{\sim}\mathfrak{t}_{2};\mathfrak{s}_{2}}\quad\textsc{right=($;$)}&\frac{\mathfrak{t}_{1}\dot{\sim}\mathfrak{t}_{2}\hskip 8.19447pt\mathfrak{s}_{1}\dot{\sim}\mathfrak{s}_{2}}{\mathfrak{t}_{1}\oplus\mathfrak{s}_{1}\dot{\sim}\mathfrak{t}_{2}\oplus\mathfrak{s}_{2}}\quad\textsc{right=($\oplus$)}&\frac{\mathfrak{t}_{1}\dot{\sim}\mathfrak{t}_{2}\hskip 8.19447pt\mathfrak{s}_{1}\dot{\sim}\mathfrak{s}_{2}}{\mathfrak{t}_{1}\otimes\mathfrak{s}_{1}\dot{\sim}\mathfrak{t}_{2}\otimes\mathfrak{s}_{2}}\quad\textsc{right=($\otimes$)}\end{array}\end{array}\@add@centering

(19)

A straightforward verification shows that the axioms are sound.

Proposition 19

(Soundness)
.

For all
\mathfrak{s},\mathfrak{t}\in\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{PB})
, if
\mathfrak{s}{\dot{\sim}}\mathfrak{t}
then
\left\llbracket\mathfrak{s}\right\rrbracket=\left\llbracket\mathfrak{t}\right\rrbracket
.

For the completeness proof, it is convenient to work with
\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{\mathbb{PB}})
rather than
\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{PB})
.
To this end, consider the functor

\mathbf{T}(Q_{\mathbb{PB}})\colon\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{PB})\to\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{\mathbb{PB}}),

obtained by applying
\mathbf{T}(-)
to the quotient functor
Q_{\mathbb{PB}}\colon\mathbf{Diag}_{PB}\to\mathbf{Diag}_{\mathbb{PB}}
, i.e., the canonical functor identifying diagrams modulo
=_{\mathbb{PB}}
.
Moreover, let
\sim
denote the congruence on
\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{\mathbb{PB}})
defined as
\dot{\sim}
but without the rule
(\mathbb{PB})
. The following result shows that reasoning with
\sim
suffices.

Proposition 20
.

For all
\mathfrak{s},\mathfrak{t}\in\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{PB})
,
\mathfrak{s}\dot{\sim}\mathfrak{t}
iff
\mathbf{T}(Q_{\mathbb{PB}})(\mathfrak{s})\sim\mathbf{T}(Q_{\mathbb{PB}})(\mathfrak{t})
.

Henceforth, we write
\mathbf{B}[1,A^{n}]
for the set of
n
-ary Boolean vectors, i.e., the set of tapes in
\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{\mathbb{PB}})[1,A^{n}]
of the form

\overrightarrow{b}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}\bigotimes_{i=1}^{n}b_{i},

The second property crucially relies on axiom (
5
) and on the monoidal enrichment in (
16
).

Lemma 22
.

For all
n\in\mathbb{N}
,
\frac{1}{2^{n}}\cdot{id}_{A^{n}}\sim\sum_{\overrightarrow{b}\in\mathbf{B}[1,A^{n}]}\frac{1}{2^{n}}\cdot\overleftarrow{b};\overrightarrow{b}
;

Note that for
n=1
, the lemma above reduces to axiom (
5
). Combining Lemma
22
and axiom (
5
) we obtain the third key result.

Lemma 23
.

Let
\mathfrak{s},\mathfrak{t}\in\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{\mathbb{PB}})[A^{n},A^{m}]
. If, for all
\overrightarrow{b}\in\mathbf{B}[1,A^{n}]
,
\overrightarrow{b};\mathfrak{s}\sim\overrightarrow{b};\mathfrak{t}
, then
\mathfrak{s}\sim\mathfrak{t}
.

7.2
Completeness

We denote by
\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{\mathbb{PB}})_{\sim}
the quotient of
\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{\mathbb{PB}})
by
\sim
, and by

Q_{\sim}\colon\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{\mathbb{PB}})\to\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{\mathbb{PB}})_{\sim}

the corresponding quotient functor. By Propositions
19
and
20
,
\left\llbracket-\right\rrbracket\colon\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{PB})\to\mathcal{KL}(\mathcal{D}_{\leq})
factors as

\textstyle{\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{PB})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\mathbf{T}(Q_{\mathbb{PB}})}
\textstyle{\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{\mathbb{PB}})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{Q_{\sim}}
\textstyle{\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{\mathbb{PB}})_{\sim}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{I}
\textstyle{\mathcal{KL}(\mathcal{D}_{\leq})}

for some functor
I
. Proving completeness amounts to showing that
I
is faithful.

Now, observe that
J\colon\,\mathbf{Par}\to\mathcal{KL}(\mathcal{D}_{\leq})
from Section
3
restricts to
J_{2}\colon\mathbf{Par}_{2}\to\mathcal{KL}(\mathcal{D}_{\leq})
. Since
\mathcal{KL}(\mathcal{D}_{\leq})
is a convex biproduct category, by the two adjunctions in (
17
), there exists a functor

J_{2}^{\prime}\colon\mathbf{StMat}(\mathbf{Par}_{2}^{+})\to\mathcal{KL}(\mathcal{D}_{\leq})\text{.}

Consider the diagram on the right, where the vertical isomorphisms are those in (
18
). Such diagram commutes, as stated by the following result where
H
is the composition of the left vertical isomorphisms with
J_{2}^{\prime}
.

Lemma 24
.

I\circ Q_{\sim}=H
.

\textstyle{\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{\mathbb{PB}})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{Q_{\sim}}
\scriptstyle{\cong}
\textstyle{\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{\mathbb{PB}})_{\sim}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{I}
\textstyle{{\mathbf{StMat}(\mathbf{Diag}_{\mathbb{PB}}^{+})}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\cong}
\textstyle{\mathbf{StMat}(\mathbf{Par}_{2}^{+})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{J_{2}^{\prime}}
\textstyle{\mathcal{KL}(\mathcal{D}_{\leq})}

We first observe that
H
is faithful for subdistributions of Boolean vectors.

Lemma 25
.

For all
\mathfrak{t},\mathfrak{t}^{\prime}\in\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{\mathbb{B}})[A^{0},A^{m}]
, if
H(\mathfrak{t})=H(\mathfrak{t}^{\prime})
, then
\mathfrak{t}=\mathfrak{t}^{\prime}
.

Moreover, by Lemma
11
, we have the following normal forms for tapes
\mathfrak{t}\colon A^{0}\to A^{m}
.

Lemma 26
.

For all
\mathfrak{t}\in\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{\mathbb{PB}})[A^{0},A^{m}]
, there exist,
p,q\in[0,1]
and for
i=1,\dots,n
,
p_{i}\in(0,1)
such that
\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}=1
, and

such that

The previous two results, combined with Lemma
21
allow us to prove the following key property.

Lemma 27
.

For all
\mathfrak{t},\mathfrak{t}^{\prime}\in\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{\mathbb{PB}})[A^{0},A^{m}]
, if
H(\mathfrak{t})=H(\mathfrak{t}^{\prime})
, then
\mathfrak{t}\sim\mathfrak{t}^{\prime}
.

Theorem 28
.

I\colon\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{\mathbb{PB}})_{\sim}\to\mathbf{StMat}(\mathcal{KL}(\mathcal{D}_{\leq})_{2})
is faithful.

Proof.

Let
[\mathfrak{t}]_{\sim},[\mathfrak{s}]_{\sim}\in\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{\mathbb{PB}})_{\sim}[A^{n},A^{m}]
be such that
I([\mathfrak{t}]_{\sim})=I([\mathfrak{s}]_{\sim})
. Then:

\displaystyle I([\mathfrak{t}]_{\sim})=I([\mathfrak{s}]_{\sim})

\displaystyle\implies H(\mathfrak{t})=H(\mathfrak{s})

(Lemma
24
)

\displaystyle\implies\text{for all }\overrightarrow{b}\in\mathbf{B}[1,A^{n}],H(\overrightarrow{b});H(\mathfrak{t})=H(\overrightarrow{b});H(\mathfrak{s})

\displaystyle\implies\text{for all }\overrightarrow{b}\in\mathbf{B}[1,A^{n}],H(\overrightarrow{b};\mathfrak{t})=H(\overrightarrow{b};\mathfrak{s})

(Functoriality)

\displaystyle\implies\text{for all }\overrightarrow{b}\in\mathbf{B}[1,A^{n}],\overrightarrow{b};\mathfrak{t}\sim\overrightarrow{b};\mathfrak{s}

(Lemma
27
)

\displaystyle\implies\mathfrak{t}\sim\mathfrak{s}

(Lemma
23
)

Hence,
[\mathfrak{t}]_{\sim}=[\mathfrak{s}]_{\sim}
. The above derivation proves that
I
is faithful for arrows of type
A^{n}\to A^{m}
. For arrows of type
A^{k}\to\bigoplus_{i=1}^{n}A^{m_{i}}
one can rely on convex products (Definition
14
) and reduce to the previous case. While for arrows of arbitrary type
\bigoplus_{j=1}^{o}A^{k_{j}}\to\bigoplus_{i=1}^{n}A^{m_{i}}
, one can easily rely on the universal property of coproducts. See Appendix
F
for all details.
∎

Corollary 29

(Completeness)
.

For all
\mathfrak{s},\mathfrak{t}\in\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{PB})
, if
\left\llbracket\mathfrak{s}\right\rrbracket=\left\llbracket\mathfrak{t}\right\rrbracket
then
\mathfrak{s}{\dot{\sim}}\mathfrak{t}
.

Corollary 30
.

For all
c,d\in\mathbf{Diag}_{PrB}
,
\langle\!\langle{c}\rangle\!\rangle=\langle\!\langle{d}\rangle\!\rangle
iff
\mathcal{E}(c){\dot{\sim}}\mathcal{E}(d)
.

8
Conclusions and Future Work

We introduced an axiomatisation of
partial
Boolean circuits (
Figures

1
and
3
) and proved it complete (
Theorem

9
). Extending this, we gave laws of
probabilistic Boolean tapes
(
Figures

4
and
5
) and, using a general result from
[
6
]
, established their completeness (
Corollary

29
). Combined with the encoding in
[
8
]
, this allows checking semantic equality of
probabilistic Boolean circuits

[
59
]
(
Corollary

30
).

+_{p}
i
t

In Example
13
, it is shown that the combined use of
\oplus
and
\otimes
allows probabilistic tapes to realise probabilistic control effectively. Extending tapes with traces for
\oplus
–following the approach of
[
9
]
, which provides a unifying account of several program logics
[
41
,
55
,
2
,
23
]
–would enable the representation of iteration and, potentially, provide algebraic foundations for probabilistic program logics
[
47
,
56
]
.
Indeed, such extended tapes can encode probabilistic regular expressions from
[
63
]
. For instance, the expression
i;c^{[p]};t

Lemma 32
.

Let
b\in\mathbf{Diag}_{B}[1,A^{n}]
and
c\in\mathbf{Diag}_{PB}[A^{n},A^{m}]
.

i.

If
\langle\!\langle{b;c}\rangle\!\rangle_{PB}=\bot
, then
\langle\!\langle{b;D_{c}}\rangle\!\rangle_{PB}=0
;

ii.

If
\langle\!\langle{b;c}\rangle\!\rangle_{PB}=\langle\!\langle{b^{\prime}}\rangle\!\rangle_{PB}
for some
b^{\prime}\in\mathbf{Diag}_{B}[1,A^{m}]
, then
\langle\!\langle{b;D_{c}}\rangle\!\rangle_{PB}=1
and
\langle\!\langle{b;T_{c}}\rangle\!\rangle_{PB}=\langle\!\langle{b^{\prime}}\rangle\!\rangle_{PB}

Proof of Proposition
10
.

Recall that
\langle\!\langle{-}\rangle\!\rangle_{PB}\colon\mathbf{Diag}_{{PB}}\to\mathbf{Par}
is defined on objects as
\langle\!\langle{A^{n}}\rangle\!\rangle_{PB}=2^{n}
. Hence for all
c\in\mathbf{Diag}_{{PB}}[A^{n},A^{m}]
,
\langle\!\langle{c}\rangle\!\rangle_{PB}\in\mathbf{Par}[2^{n},2^{m}]
, namely

\langle\!\langle{c}\rangle\!\rangle_{PB}
is an arrow of
\mathbf{Par}_{2}
. Thus
\langle\!\langle{-}\rangle\!\rangle_{PB}\colon\mathbf{Diag}_{{PB}}\to\mathbf{Par}
factors as

\textstyle{\mathbf{Diag}_{PB}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\textstyle{\mathbf{Par}_{2}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\textstyle{\mathbf{Par}}
.

Moreover, by soundness (Proposition
3
), it factors through
\mathbf{Diag}_{{\mathbb{PB}}}
:

\textstyle{\mathbf{Diag}_{PB}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\textstyle{\mathbf{Diag}_{\mathbb{PB}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\textstyle{\mathbf{Par}_{2}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\textstyle{\mathbf{Par}}

The central functor is faithful by completeness. To conclude that it is an isomorphism, it is enough to prove fullness, i.e., that for any partial function
f\colon 2^{n}\to 2^{m}
, there exists some diagram
d\colon A^{n}\to A^{m}
such that
\langle\!\langle{d}\rangle\!\rangle_{PB}=f
. But this is trivial by first observing that for any such partial function, there exist total functions
D_{f}\colon 2^{n}\to 2
and
T_{f}\colon 2^{n}\to 2^{m}
that decompose
f
as in Proposition
6
and then make use of Proposition
31
.
∎

Proof of Proposition
19
.

Since the axioms in
\mathbb{PB}
are sounds with respect to
\langle\!\langle{-}\rangle\!\rangle
and since
\langle\!\langle{-}\rangle\!\rangle=\left\llbracket\mathcal{E}(-)\right\rrbracket
, these axioms are also sound for
\left\llbracket-\right\rrbracket
.
For (
5
) and (
5
), it enough to check that the left and the right hand sides are mapped into the same
\mathcal{KL}(\mathcal{D}_{\leq})
-arrows by
\left\llbracket-\right\rrbracket
.
For (
5
), it is enough to observe that cancellativity holds in
\mathcal{KL}(\mathcal{D}_{\leq})
.
∎

Consider the congruence
\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}
on
\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{PB})
generated by the rules in (
20
)

\centering\begin{array}[]{c}\begin{array}[]{c@{\qquad\qquad}c@{\qquad\qquad}c@{\qquad\qquad}c}\frac{c=_{\mathbb{PB}}d}{\overline{\underline{\;c\vphantom{d_{A}}\;}}\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}\overline{\underline{\;d\vphantom{d_{A}}\;}}}\quad\textsc{right=($\mathbb{PB}$)}&\frac{-}{\mathfrak{t}\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}\mathfrak{t}}\quad\textsc{right=($\textsc{R}$)}&\frac{\mathfrak{t}_{1}\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}\mathfrak{t}_{2}}{\mathfrak{t}_{2}\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}\mathfrak{t}_{1}}\quad\textsc{right=($\textsc{S}$)}&\frac{\mathfrak{t}_{1}\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}\mathfrak{t}_{2}\hskip 8.19447pt\mathfrak{t}_{2}\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}\mathfrak{t}_{3}}{\mathfrak{t}_{1}\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}\mathfrak{t}_{3}}\quad\textsc{right=($\textsc{T}$)}\end{array}\\[10.0pt]
\begin{array}[]{c@{\qquad}c@{\qquad}c}\frac{\mathfrak{t}_{1}\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}\mathfrak{t}_{2}\hskip 8.19447pt\mathfrak{s}_{1}\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}\mathfrak{s}_{2}}{\mathfrak{t}_{1};\mathfrak{s}_{1}\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}\mathfrak{t}_{2};\mathfrak{s}_{2}}\quad\textsc{right=($;$)}&\frac{\mathfrak{t}_{1}\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}\mathfrak{t}_{2}\hskip 8.19447pt\mathfrak{s}_{1}\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}\mathfrak{s}_{2}}{\mathfrak{t}_{1}\oplus\mathfrak{s}_{1}\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}\mathfrak{t}_{2}\oplus\mathfrak{s}_{2}}\quad\textsc{right=($\oplus$)}&\frac{\mathfrak{t}_{1}\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}\mathfrak{t}_{2}\hskip 8.19447pt\mathfrak{s}_{1}\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}\mathfrak{s}_{2}}{\mathfrak{t}_{1}\otimes\mathfrak{s}_{1}\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}\mathfrak{t}_{2}\otimes\mathfrak{s}_{2}}\quad\textsc{right=($\otimes$)}\end{array}\end{array}\@add@centering

(20)

Proposition 33
.

For all
\mathfrak{s},\mathfrak{t}\in\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{PB})
,
\mathfrak{s}\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}\mathfrak{t}
iff
\mathbf{T}(Q_{\mathbb{PB}})(\mathfrak{s})=\mathbf{T}(Q_{\mathbb{PB}})(\mathfrak{t})
.

Proof.

Let
\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{PB})_{\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}}
be the quotient of
\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{PB})
by
\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}
: objects are those of
\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{PB})
, arrows are
\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}
-equivalence classes of arrows of
\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{PB})
, hereafter denoted by
[\mathfrak{t}]_{\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}}
. We prove that
\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{PB})_{\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}}
is isomorphic to
\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{\mathbb{PB}})
.

We first define the functor
F\colon\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{PB})_{\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}}\to\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{\mathbb{PB}})
inductively as

\begin{array}[]{ccccc}F(^{p}\!\!\lhd_{U})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}\;^{p}\!\!\lhd_{U}&F(\,\!\rotatebox{90.0}{$\multimapinv$}_{U})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}\!\rotatebox{90.0}{$\multimapinv$}_{U}&F(\underline{\smash{\overline{\;c\vphantom{t}\;}}})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}\underline{\smash{\overline{\;[c]_{\mathbb{PB}}\vphantom{t}\;}}}&F(\rotatebox{90.0}{$\multimap$}_{U})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}\rotatebox{90.0}{$\multimap$}_{U}&F(\rhd_{U})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}\rhd_{U}\\
F({id}_{U})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}{id}_{U}&F({id}_{0})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}{id}_{0}&F(\sigma_{U,V}^{\oplus})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}\sigma_{U,V}^{\oplus}&F(\mathfrak{t}_{1};\mathfrak{t}_{2})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}F(\mathfrak{t}_{1});F(\mathfrak{t}_{2})&F(\mathfrak{t}_{1}\oplus\mathfrak{t}_{2})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}F(\mathfrak{t}_{1})\oplus F(\mathfrak{t}_{2})\end{array}

Since arrows in
\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{PB})_{\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}}
are
\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}
-equivalence classes, we need to prove that the functor is well-defined, namely that if
\mathfrak{s}\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}\mathfrak{t}
then
F(\mathfrak{s})=F(\mathfrak{t})
. This is done by induction on the rules in (
20
). For the case of the rule (
\mathbb{PB}
), observe that
\mathfrak{s}=\overline{\underline{\;c\vphantom{d_{A}}\;}}
,
\mathfrak{t}=\overline{\underline{\;d\vphantom{d_{A}}\;}}
and
c=_{\mathbb{PB}}d
. By the definition of
F
,
F(\mathfrak{s})=F(\mathfrak{t})
. All the other cases are trivial, with the only exception of the rule
(\otimes)
where one observes that, since
=_{\mathbb{PB}}
is a congruence w.r.t.
\otimes
, then
F
is a morphism of rig categories.

The functor
G\colon\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{\mathbb{PB}})\to\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{PB})_{\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}}
is defined on
\underline{\smash{\overline{\;[c]_{\mathbb{PB}}\vphantom{t}\;}}}
as
G(\underline{\smash{\overline{\;[c]_{\mathbb{PB}}\vphantom{t}\;}}})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}[\underline{\smash{\overline{\;c\vphantom{t}\;}}}]_{\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}}
and then inductively in the same style of the functor
F
above. Observe that
F(G(\underline{\smash{\overline{\;[c]_{\mathbb{PB}}\vphantom{t}\;}}}))=\underline{\smash{\overline{\;[c]_{\mathbb{PB}}\vphantom{t}\;}}}
and
G(F([\underline{\smash{\overline{\;c\vphantom{t}\;}}}]_{\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}}))=[\underline{\smash{\overline{\;c\vphantom{t}\;}}}]_{\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}}
. A simple inductive argument confirms that
F
and
G
are inverses of each other.
∎

Proof of Proposition
20
.

We first prove by induction on the rules in (
19
) that if
\mathfrak{s}\dot{\sim}\mathfrak{t}
then
\mathbf{T}(Q_{\mathbb{PB}})(\mathfrak{s})\sim\mathbf{T}(Q_{\mathbb{PB}})(\mathfrak{t})
.
Consider the case of the rule
(\mathbb{PB})
: in this case
\mathfrak{s}=\underline{\smash{\overline{\;c\vphantom{t}\;}}}
,
\mathfrak{t}=\underline{\smash{\overline{\;d\vphantom{t}\;}}}
and
c=_{\scalebox{0.6}{$\mathbb{PB}$}}d
. Thus
\mathbf{T}(Q_{\mathbb{PB}})(\mathfrak{s})=\mathbf{T}(Q_{\mathbb{PB}})(\mathfrak{t})
.
All the other cases trivially follow from the fact that
\mathbf{T}(Q_{\mathbb{PB}})
is a morphism of rig categories: see
[
8
]
.

Again, by induction on the rules, we prove that if
\mathbf{T}(Q_{\mathbb{PB}})(\mathfrak{s})\sim\mathbf{T}(Q_{\mathbb{PB}})(\mathfrak{t})
then
\mathfrak{s}\dot{\sim}\mathfrak{t}
.
Here the only non-trivial cases are
(R)
,
(
5
)
and
(
5
)
. For
(R)
, if
\mathbf{T}(Q_{\mathbb{PB}})(\mathfrak{s})=\mathbf{T}(Q_{\mathbb{PB}})(\mathfrak{t})
, then by Proposition
33
,
\mathfrak{s}\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}\mathfrak{t}
. Hence,
\mathfrak{s}\dot{\sim}\mathfrak{t}
. For
(
5
)
, if
\mathbf{T}(Q_{\mathbb{PB}})(\mathfrak{s})\overset{\eqref{ax:AXPBP1}}{=}\mathbf{T}(Q_{\mathbb{PB}})(\mathfrak{t})
, then
\mathfrak{s}
is
\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}
-equivalent to the left hand side of (
5
) and
\mathfrak{t}
is
\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}
-equivalent to the right hand side of (
5
). Hence, they are
\dot{\sim}
-equivalent, and applying transitivity of
\dot{\sim}
, we conclude that
\mathfrak{s}\dot{\sim}\mathfrak{t}
. The case of
(
5
)
is analogous.
∎

((
4
))

\displaystyle=\star_{A^{0},A^{n}}.

(Def. of
\star
)

∎

proof of Lemma
22
.

By induction on
n
. The base case is trivial. For the inductive step, we have

\displaystyle\frac{1}{2^{n+1}}\cdot{id}_{A^{n+1}}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2^{n}}\frac{1}{2}\cdot({id}_{A}\otimes{id}_{A^{n}})

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2^{n}}\cdot\left(\frac{1}{2}\cdot{id}_{A}\otimes{id}_{A^{n}}\right)

((
16
))

\displaystyle=(\frac{1}{2}\cdot{id}_{A})\otimes(\frac{1}{2^{n}}\cdot{id}_{A^{n}})

((

Proof of Lemma
24
.

In order to prove the statement we exploit Proposition
33
which provides an isomorphism
F\colon\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{PB})_{\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}}\to\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{\mathbb{PB}})
, such that
Q_{\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}};F={\mathbf{T}(Q_{\mathbb{PB}})}
, where
Q_{\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}}\colon\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{PB})\to\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{PB})_{\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}}
is the quotient functor.
Then, since
\left\llbracket-\right\rrbracket
is clearly sound with respect to
{\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}}
, it is enough to prove that
H\circ F\circ Q_{\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}}=\left\llbracket-\right\rrbracket
. Since
\left\llbracket-\right\rrbracket
is defined inductively, it is enough to check that
H\circ F\circ Q_{\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}}
and
\left\llbracket-\right\rrbracket
coincide on generators.
For instance consider the generator
{}^{p}\!\!\lhd_{A^{n}}
:

\displaystyle H\circ F\circ Q_{\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}}(^{p}\!\!\lhd_{A^{n}})

\displaystyle=H\circ F(^{p}\!\!\lhd_{A^{n}})

(Def.
Q_{\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}}
)

\displaystyle=H(^{p}\!\!\lhd_{A^{n}})

(Def.
F
)

\displaystyle=L^{\flat}(^{p}\!\!\lhd_{A^{n}})

(Lemma
34
)

\displaystyle=\,^{p}\!\!\lhd_{2^{n}}

(
21
)

\displaystyle=\left\llbracket{}^{p}\!\!\lhd_{A^{n}}\right\rrbracket.

(Def.
\left\llbracket-\right\rrbracket
)

The cases for the generators
\!\rotatebox{90.0}{$\multimapinv$}_{A^{n}}
,
\rotatebox{90.0}{$\multimap$}_{A^{n}}
and
\rhd_{A^{n}}
are analogous. For the generator
\underline{\smash{\overline{\;c\vphantom{t}\;}}}
, we have

\displaystyle H\circ F\circ Q_{\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}}(\underline{\smash{\overline{\;c\vphantom{t}\;}}})

\displaystyle=H\circ F([\underline{\smash{\overline{\;c\vphantom{t}\;}}}]_{\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}})

(Def.
Q_{\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}}
)

\displaystyle=H(\underline{\smash{\overline{\;[c]_{\mathbb{PB}}\vphantom{t}\;}}})

(Def.
F
)

\displaystyle=L^{\flat}(\underline{\smash{\overline{\;[c]_{\mathbb{PB}}\vphantom{t}\;}}})

(Lemma
34
)

\displaystyle=L([c]_{\mathbb{PB}})

(
21
)

\displaystyle=J_{2}(\langle\!\langle{c}\rangle\!\rangle_{PB})

(Proposition
10
)

\displaystyle=\left\llbracket\underline{\smash{\overline{\;c\vphantom{t}\;}}}\right\rrbracket.

(Def.
\left\llbracket-\right\rrbracket
)

The remaining cases are trivial.
Hence, by the universal property of

\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{PB})_{\doteq_{\mathbb{PB}}}
we obtain that
H\circ F=I\circ Q_{\sim}\circ F
, and since

is an isomorphism, we obtain the statement.

∎

Proof of Lemma

.

). By construction, it is the identity-on-objects functor sending a subdistribution

, where

in (
17
), and that fact that the isomorphisms

restricted to

factor through the composition

and the obvious isomorphism

.
∎

Additional details for the proof of Theorem
28
.

In the main text we have already proved that
I
is faithful for arrows of type
A^{n}\to A^{m}
.
This fact and convex products easily entail that
I
is faithful for arrows
\mathfrak{s},\mathfrak{t}\colon A^{k}\to\bigoplus_{i=1}^{n}A^{m_{i}}
.
Indeed, by Theorem
16
,

\mathfrak{s}=\langle\mathfrak{s}_{1},\dots,\mathfrak{s}_{n}\rangle_{\vec{q}}\quad\mathfrak{t}=\langle\mathfrak{t}_{1},\dots,\mathfrak{t}_{n}\rangle_{\vec{p}}

(24)

for some
\vec{q}=q_{1},\dots,q_{n}
,
\vec{p}=p_{1},\dots,p_{n}
,
\mathfrak{s}_{i}\colon A^{k}\to A^{m_{i}}
and
\mathfrak{t}_{i}\colon A^{k}\to A^{m_{i}}
. Thus

\displaystyle I([\mathfrak{s}]_{\sim})=I([\mathfrak{t}]_{\sim})

\displaystyle\Rightarrow H(\mathfrak{s})=H(\mathfrak{t})

(Lemma
24
)

\displaystyle\Rightarrow\text{for all }j\text{, }H(\mathfrak{s});H(\pi_{j})=H(\mathfrak{t});H(\pi_{j})

\displaystyle\Rightarrow\text{for all }j\text{, }H(\mathfrak{s};\pi_{j})=H(\mathfrak{t};\pi_{j})

(Functoriality)

\displaystyle\Rightarrow\text{for all }j\text{, }\mathfrak{s};\pi_{j}\sim\mathfrak{t};\pi_{j}

(Previous implication)

\displaystyle\Rightarrow\text{for all }j\text{, }q_{j}\cdot\mathfrak{s}_{j}\sim p_{j}\cdot\mathfrak{t}_{j}

(
24
)

\displaystyle\Rightarrow\text{for all }j\text{, }[q_{j}\cdot\mathfrak{s}_{j}]_{\sim}=[p_{j}\cdot\mathfrak{t}_{j}]_{\sim}

Now
[
6
, Proposition 6]
states that
\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{\mathbb{PB}})_{\sim}
is a convex biproduct category and that the quotient functor
Q_{\sim}\colon\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{\mathbb{PB}})\to\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{\mathbb{PB}})_{\sim}
is a morphism of convex biproduct categories. Hence,
[
7
, Corollary 4]
implies that
(\bigoplus_{j=1}^{n}A^{m_{j}},[\pi_{j}]_{\sim})
is the
n
-ary convex product of
A^{m_{1}},\dots,A^{m_{n}}
in
\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{\mathbb{PB}})_{\sim}
and
[\mathfrak{s}]_{\sim}
is the unique arrow such that for all
j=1,\dots,n
,

\displaystyle[\mathfrak{s}]_{\sim};[\pi_{j}]_{\sim}

\displaystyle=[\mathfrak{s};\pi_{j}]_{\sim}

(Functoriality of
Q_{\sim}
)

\displaystyle=[q_{j}\cdot\mathfrak{s}_{j}]_{\sim}

(
24
)

\displaystyle=q_{j}\cdot[\mathfrak{s}_{j}]_{\sim};

(pca-enrichment of
\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{\mathbb{PB}})_{\sim}
)

while
[\mathfrak{t}]_{\sim}
is the unique arrow such that for all
j=1,\dots,n
,

\displaystyle[\mathfrak{t}]_{\sim};[\pi_{j}]_{\sim}

\displaystyle=[\mathfrak{t};\pi_{j}]_{\sim}

(Functoriality of
Q_{\sim}
)

\displaystyle=[p_{j}\cdot\mathfrak{t}_{j}]_{\sim}

(
24
)

\displaystyle=p_{j}\cdot[\mathfrak{t}_{j}]_{\sim}.

(pca-enrichment of
\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{Diag}_{\mathbb{PB}})_{\sim}
)

Hence, since for all
j=1,\dots,n
,
[q_{j}\cdot\mathfrak{s}_{j}]_{\sim}=[p_{j}\cdot\mathfrak{t}_{j}]_{\sim}
, we have
[\mathfrak{s}]_{\sim}=[\mathfrak{t}]_{\sim}
.

For arrows of arbitrary type
\bigoplus_{j=1}^{o}A^{k_{j}}\to\bigoplus_{i=1}^{n}A^{m_{i}}
, one can easily rely on the universal property of coproducts and the case that we just proved.
∎

Proof of Corollary
29
.

By Theorem
28
,
I
is faithful. The following derivation concludes the proof.

\displaystyle\left\llbracket\mathfrak{s}\right\rrbracket=\left\llbracket\mathfrak{t}\right\rrbracket

\displaystyle\Longleftrightarrow(\mathbf{T}(Q_{\mathbb{PB}});Q_{\sim};I)(\mathfrak{s})=(\mathbf{T}(Q_{\mathbb{PB}});Q_{\sim};I)(\mathfrak{t})

(
\left\llbracket-\right\rrbracket=\mathbf{T}(Q_{\mathbb{PB}});Q_{\sim};I
)

\displaystyle\implies(\mathbf{T}(Q_{\mathbb{PB}});Q_{\sim})(\mathfrak{s})=(\mathbf{T}(Q_{\mathbb{PB}});Q_{\sim})(\mathfrak{t})

(
I
is faithful)

\displaystyle\Longleftrightarrow\mathbf{T}(Q_{\mathbb{PB}})(\mathfrak{s})\sim\mathbf{T}(Q_{\mathbb{PB}})(\mathfrak{t})

(Def.
Q_{\sim}
)

\displaystyle\Longleftrightarrow\mathfrak{s}\dot{\sim}\mathfrak{t}

(Proposition
20
)

∎

Proof of Corollary
30
.

\displaystyle\langle\!\langle{c}\rangle\!\rangle=\langle\!\langle{d}\rangle\!\rangle

\displaystyle\Longleftrightarrow\left\llbracket\mathcal{E}(c)\right\rrbracket=\left\llbracket\mathcal{E}(d)\right\rrbracket

(Proposition
12
)

\displaystyle\Longleftrightarrow\mathcal{E}(c){\dot{\sim}}\mathcal{E}(d).

(Proposition
19
, Corollary
29
)

∎
